Avert

uh-VURT -- Latin ab- ('away') plus vertere ('to turn'): to turn danger away before it lands. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To avert is to prevent something bad, or to turn away one's eyes.

The signal operator's quick thinking helped avert a head-on train collision.

Worked Example

Noticing a hairline crack in the dam wall, an engineer orders the reservoir drained overnight -- and by morning, the flood that would have drowned the valley never happens.

Stopping a disaster before it strikes is exactly what it means to avert. Unlike 'survive,' which means enduring a disaster that happens, avert means making sure it never happens at all.

How Avert Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

avoid

avoid: to keep away from something

forestall

forestall: to prevent something by acting first

prevent

prevent: to stop something from happening

Antonyms

cause

cause: to make something happen

invite

invite: to bring something on, often unintentionally

How Strong Is It? — avoid → avert → forestall

avoid vs. avert

avoid vs. avert: Avoid is looser than avert -- you avoid something by staying clear of it yourself, while to avert is to actively turn the danger aside so it strikes no one.

forestall vs. avert

forestall vs. avert: Forestall is a more strategic sibling of avert: to avert is to turn away a looming harm, while to forestall is to act so early that the threat never even takes shape.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — a-

prefix — a-: away from (variant of Latin ab-)

root — -vert

root — -vert: to turn (Latin (vertere))

Put it together

Put it together: Latin avertere meant 'to turn away,' from ab- ('away', worn down to a-) and vertere ('to turn') -- you avert your eyes or avert a crisis by turning it aside, the same root that gives us divert and this unit's averse.

Use the root in a new word: divert

Use the root in a new word: divert: Police set up cones to divert traffic around the parade route.

Root Check

Word Choice

Avert pairs most often with dangers -- 'avert a crisis,' 'avert disaster' -- and with eyes: to 'avert your gaze' is to turn it away. Don't confuse the verb avert with this unit's adjective averse ('averse to risk').
